sections.html:
Down in southern Dakota County, Farmington marks the metro's outer rim. Population is 25,425, up 7.4 percent since April 2020, spread over roughly 14.6 square miles. Lakeville borders it on the west, and Empire Township lies to the east.

Owners live in 86.5 percent of the housing units, and the middle owner-occupied home is valued at $366,200. Your competition is mostly other single-family houses. The city has 8,313 households of 2.85 people each. Household income sits at $123,673, rent at $1,241 and the drive to work at 27.7 minutes. Monthly owner costs run $2,175 with a mortgage and $781 without, handy numbers if a buyer wonders what the place costs to carry.

County Highway 50 splits the town in two for most residents. The older downtown is south of it, newer subdivisions are north of it, and more growth is spreading east into Empire Township. A trail along the Vermillion River links downtown, uptown and the Empire-side neighborhoods, and deserves a mention in your listing.

Before closing, phone Farmington Utility Billing (651-280-6883) and book a final meter reading. Water is not turned off when you move out, so the account runs until you end it.

  • Bills arrive quarterly and cover water, sewer, storm water and street lights.
  • Trash and recycling come from Dick's Sanitation, which takes cancellations at 952-469-2239.
  • An unpaid final bill is certified to the property as a special assessment, and an open account can lead the title company to hold funds back at closing.

Landlords should know that rental utility accounts stay in the owner's name, so the closing falls to you rather than the tenant. Rental accounts that fall behind carry a late fee of 10 percent. Request the exact closing-day balance from Utility Billing instead of relying on the last bill.

sections.h2: Schools and neighborhoods buyers ask about
sections.html:
Farmington is in Independent School District 192, which enrolls about 6,900 students. The attendance area also takes in eastern Lakeville and the surrounding townships, so check which district serves your street before writing the listing.

Condition questions vary by area. Subdivisions north of County Highway 50 are mostly under twenty years old, while downtown houses are older and more likely to need updated systems. Main routes are Minnesota Highways 3 and 50 and Dakota County Roads 31 and 50.

sections.h2: Ways to sell a Farmington house
sections.html:
• Agent listing: best for a house in good shape, if you can wait through inspections and loan approval.
  • Do it yourself: saves the commission, but you take on marketing, paperwork and negotiation.
  • Cash buyer: suits inherited houses, put-off repairs, rentals with tenants and owners behind on payments. The buyer accepts the house in its present state, and you set the closing date.

On any route, Minnesota Statutes 513.55 has you hand over a written disclosure of known material facts before the purchase agreement. Repairs are not part of that duty. Cash buyers take the house as it stands, while retail buyers often negotiate fixes after an inspection.

sections.h2: Filing the deed in Dakota County
sections.html:
Every Farmington deed goes through the county records office in Hastings. Walk-in filing needs an appointment at the Administration Center, and mailed packets go to 1590 Highway 55 in Hastings with a return envelope. Most parcels countywide are abstract property, so your title company will search the record before closing.

Minnesota's deed tax is the net sale price times 0.0033. The deed must include a well disclosure certificate or a statement that the seller knows of no wells (Minnesota Statutes 103I.235). The auditor also looks for delinquent taxes first (Minnesota Statutes 272.12). Fees come from state law and appear on the county's fee page, and your title company can quote the sum.

sections.h2: Property tax due dates and penalties
sections.html:
Two installments make up the Dakota County bill (Minnesota Statutes 279.01). Miss one and the penalty is 2 percent for a homestead or 4 percent for other property, growing monthly through December.

Dakota County property tax installments
InstallmentDue datePenalty if missed
First halfMay 152 percent homestead, 4 percent other
Second halfOctober 152 percent homestead, 4 percent other

The settlement statement usually divides the year's bill between buyer and seller by closing date. Search your parcel on the county website for open balances before you list. Homestead applications are due December 31.

Owe back taxes? Dakota County Property Taxation and Records can give you the payoff amount. Your latest statement confirms the parcel number and what is already paid.

The disclosure law does not make you fix the house first. It makes you say what you know. List any leaks, past basement water, aging systems and work in progress, and hand the list over before the purchase agreement. A cash buyer reads the same list and prices around it, so small fixes done only to sell are often wasted effort. A line item you disclose is far safer than one a buyer finds later. If you are selling a house with tenants or a rental history, include the lease terms and any repair requests they made. Photos of recent work, dated receipts, a copy of the survey and a short note on each system's age give buyers confidence and cut down on late haggling.

sections.h2: Gathering what the title company needs
sections.html: Set out the tax statement, parcel number, lease and keys ahead of time, and for a rental add the utility account details. Most county parcels are abstract property, so the title company will order a search of the record and may ask about old liens or easements. Answer fast, since slow replies push a closing date back. Also tell the buyer about the trail, the school district and anything about the street that affects daily life.

sections.h2: How quickly can a sale close?
sections.html: With cash, you choose the closing date, and it often lands within a few weeks since no lender appraisal is needed. An agent listing usually takes more time. For either path, schedule the water meter reading in advance and ask the county for your tax payoff figure. On the day, the title company pays off any mortgage and taxes owed, and the deed goes to the records office in Hastings.

faqs.q: How quickly can I close on a Farmington house?
faqs.a: A cash purchase can close on a date you choose, frequently within a few weeks, since no lender appraisal is involved. Listing with an agent generally runs longer. For either path, book the water meter reading with Farmington Utility Billing in advance.

faqs.q: Do I have to make repairs before I sell in Farmington?
faqs.a: No. The disclosure statute asks for a written statement of material facts you know, and repairs are not part of it. Cash buyers take the house as it stands, and retail buyers often negotiate fixes after an inspection.

faqs.q: What happens to an unpaid Farmington utility bill after a sale?
faqs.a: It stays attached to the property. The city certifies unpaid water, sewer, storm drainage and street light charges as a special assessment, so buyers' title companies usually want the last bill settled. A final meter read keeps the number accurate.

faqs.q: Who files the deed for a Farmington sale?
faqs.a: Dakota County's records office in Hastings, normally through your title company. The deed tax is 0.0033 of the net price, and the deed needs either a well certificate or a no-wells statement. The state sets the fees.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Farmington rental while tenants live there?
faqs.a: Yes. Go over the lease terms with the buyer and your title company. Rental utility accounts stay in the owner's name, so plan to close yours on the sale date.
